title: Expanding the AI Evaluation Toolbox with Statistical Models
author: Drew Keller · Kweku Kwegyir-Aggrey · Ryan Steed · Anita K. Rao · Julia L. Sharp · A. Stevie Bergman

qs: On the Information Value of AI Benchmarks for Practitioners.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The supplied material is only a bibliography. Although it cites work on statistical uncertainty, nondeterminism, benchmark defects and measurement validity that is relevant to the cluster, it provides no findings or reasoning showing whether the source accepts the proposition that credible evaluation must test professional task execution or how realistic tasks and automated judging should be validated.

st.t: Evaluation validity: Benchmark safeguards impose trade-offs
st.an: The source accepts that benchmark scores have limited transfer and should not be treated as straightforward evidence of broader performance. It materially develops the cluster’s statistical-validity component by identifying invalid uncertainty estimates and proposing generalized linear mixed models to distinguish performance concepts and improve estimation, while not addressing the cluster’s wider safeguards such as contamination, workflow validity, cost or independent safety testing.
qs: For example, some studies have shown that an increase in a system’s benchmark score does not always correspond to an increase in the system’s performance on other tasks similar to those in the benchmark [8, 9], undermining a common interpretation of benchmark results.
We then analyzed these data with a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM), which leverages data across LLMs to provide accurate and precise performance estimates.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s governance and evaluation proposition. It shows why aggregate benchmark scores are insufficient and supplies a concrete statistical framework for defining estimands, modelling item-level variation, quantifying uncertainty, checking assumptions and tailoring evaluation to the benchmark and intended inference. It does not directly address legal-work redesign or deployment outcomes, but strengthens the cluster’s account of rigorous, context-specific evaluation.
qs: Ultimately, the statistical validity of LLM evaluations benefits from evaluators explicitly adopting a model for analyzing evaluation results — whether the GLMM, a regression-free model, or something else — and disclosing related assumptions.
Reporting only a single  aggregate score misses the opportunity to analyze differences between benchmark subdivisions such as task, category, or language.

kp.k: Statistical validity requires explicit evaluation assumptions
kp.d: This cross-domain study addresses AI benchmarking rather than legal services. The authors argue that performance statistics and uncertainty estimates must be selected according to evaluation goals and data structure. Their contribution concerns statistical validity, not a resolution of the separate concerns about benchmarks' construct validity or ability to predict real-world performance.
qs: There is no one-size-fits-all formula for quantifying performance in an evaluation.

In this context, statistical validity is the extent to which reported statistical conclusions about evaluation results, including quantifications of uncertainty, are supported by assumptions and available data.

kp.k: Benchmark accuracy and generalized accuracy measure different quantities
kp.d: Benchmark accuracy is expected performance on the fixed tested items; generalized accuracy is expected performance over the related item superpopulation. Their point estimates typically resemble one another, but generalized accuracy uncertainty also incorporates item selection. Accuracy on an average-difficulty item is a third, distinct quantity. The authors recommend choosing the estimand based on evaluation purposes and defensible assumptions, not preferred error-bar size.
qs: Benchmark Accuracy — How well does the LLM perform on this specific, fixed benchmark? This notion does not automatically generalize to similar items not included in the benchmark.
Generalized Accuracy — How well would the LLM perform across the larger population of items similar to those in the benchmark?

An important nuance is that, under the model described in Eq. (1), generalized accuracy does not necessarily equal “average-item accuracy”, or an LLM’s expected score on a single item with mean difficulty with respect to the item superpopulation.

kp.k: Repeated trials require uncertainty calculations respecting item clustering
kp.d: The authors encourage multiple independent attempts to capture nondeterministic outputs, particularly on smaller benchmarks, but warn against treating every item-trial observation as independent. Dividing the standard deviation across all observations by the square root of items times trials generally overstates benchmark-accuracy uncertainty and understates generalized-accuracy uncertainty. Additional trials cannot eliminate uncertainty arising from which items entered the benchmark.
qs: The naive calculation will produce uncertainty estimates that are too large (i.e., under-confident) for benchmark accuracy estimates and too small (i.e., overconfident) for generalized accuracy estimates.
more trials do not reduce the variance due to item sampling.

kp.k: GLMMs separate system capability from item difficulty
kp.d: The proposed binomial generalized linear mixed model combines each LLM's fixed capability effect with an item's random difficulty effect through a logistic function. Items are assumed to have normally distributed difficulties; tested LLMs are treated as a fixed population. The approach resembles Rasch or one-parameter item response modeling, assumes equal item discrimination, and pools information across systems and items to support accuracy estimation and explanatory analysis.
qs: Each θi is a fixed effect that models LLM i’s latent capability to solve relevant items.
Each δ j is a random effect which estimates the difficulty of item j.
Our approach can be viewed as a variant of the Rasch model, which assumes that all items are equally discriminating [30].

kp.k: Experiments combine simulations with three multiple-choice benchmarks
kp.d: The study evaluates 22 commercially available API-access LLM systems using GPQA-Diamond, BIG-Bench Hard and Global-MMLU Lite. GPQA-Diamond contains 198 items and receives eight independent trials per item; the other benchmarks receive five. Evaluations use Inspect AI, a step-by-step multiple-choice prompt and randomized answer order. BIG-Bench Hard coverage excludes open-answer tasks. Simulations separately test a correctly specified logistic structure, a linear probability structure and a setting without latent structure.
qs: we evaluated 22 LLMs on 3 common multiple-choice benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, BIG-Bench Hard, and Global-MMLU Lite)
We ran 8 (GPQA-Diamond) or 5 (BIG-Bench Hard, Global-MMLU Lite) independent trials for each benchmark item (sample).
For BIG-Bench Hard, we only evaluated multiple-choice tasks, excluding open answer tasks such as Dyck Languages.

kp.k: Well-specified GLMMs often produce narrower confidence intervals
kp.d: In simulations matching the GLMM assumptions, generalized-accuracy estimates have similar error and approximately nominal coverage compared with regression-free estimates, while confidence intervals are often narrower and less variable. Table 8's baseline reports regression-free versus GLMM RMSE of 0.0413 versus 0.041, coverage of 0.946 versus 0.94, and mean interval width of 0.165 versus 0.153. GPQA-Diamond likewise produces similar point estimates and mostly narrower GLMM intervals. Benefits diminish with increasing benchmark size and are not universal across simulation conditions.
qs: In the well-specified Setting A, the two methods obtain very similar RMSE and both achieve close to target coverage of 95 %
Though point estimates are very similar, most GLMM CIs are narrower than regression-free CIs.
However, these gains diminish as the number of benchmark items increases

kp.k: Misspecification can undermine GLMM confidence-interval coverage
kp.d: Efficiency gains are conditional rather than guaranteed. In Setting C, where success probabilities lack the assumed latent structure, Table 7 reports identical RMSE of 0.0435 for both approaches but coverage of 0.867 for GLMM versus 0.952 for regression-free estimation. The authors report GLMM coverage in the 80–90% range for many such conditions, while regression-free methods remain near their 95% target. They recommend examining model fit and residuals.
qs: GLMM coverage also stays near the target level in Setting B, but does mildly degrade in Setting C — into the 80-90 % range for many of our simulation conditions.
Regression-free methods achieve close to target coverage across all settings.
To check model fit, we recommend common techniques like checking goodness-of-fit statistics and model residuals.

kp.k: Item difficulty estimates can flag problematic benchmark questions
kp.d: The authors present random effects as diagnostic aids, not proof that an item is defective. A BIG-Bench Hard date question has estimated difficulty δ = 7.58 and is answered incorrectly by all tested LLMs; the authors identify ambiguous wording that appears to permit either option C or E. An easy sports question has δ = −3.17 and is answered correctly by all systems. Partial pooling stabilizes difficulty estimates while accounting for differing system capabilities.
qs: Such an extreme positive random effect could indicate a truly challenging question, or that the corresponding question is problematic and should be removed from the benchmark.
Indeed, the question is ambiguously worded such that either (C) or (E) seems to be a reasonable answer.
random effects stabilize item difficulty estimates via partial pooling across LLMs while accounting for differing LLM capabilities.

kp.k: Human difficulty labels weakly track tested LLM difficulty
kp.d: For GPQA-Diamond, Chemistry's 93 items have mean estimated random effect 0.59, versus −0.37 for Biology's 19 and −0.55 for Physics's 86. The authors interpret Chemistry as harder for the tested systems, despite approximately similar proportions of human-annotated difficulty categories across domains. Substantial overlap across human difficulty categories suggests either differences between human and LLM difficulty or weaknesses in the annotations; the study does not establish which explanation is correct.
qs: Our results indicate that Chemistry items in GPQA- Diamond may be more difficult for LLMs than Physics and Biology items.
Estimated random effect distributions suggest a weak relation between writer-perceived difficulty and item difficulty for LLMs, with a large degree of item-level overlap.

kp.k: Variance decomposition informs evaluation design beyond average scores
kp.d: Between-item difficulty variation and within-item response variability distinguish systems that are consistently right or wrong on particular questions from systems that answer the same question inconsistently. For BIG-Bench Hard Movie Recommendation, σ² = 16, ICC = 0.83 and effective samples per trial = 0.23; five trials provide only slightly more information than one independent trial. Web of Lies instead has σ² = 0.47, ICC = 0.12 and effective samples per trial = 0.67. The authors recommend more unique items when between-item variation dominates and more trials when within-item variation dominates.
qs: For tasks where intra-item variance is larger, increasing trials per item may meaningfully reduce variance of accuracy estimates, while for tasks with larger inter-item variance it is more important to increase the number of unique items.
Notably, these patterns do not strongly correlate with average score, so inspecting score or accuracy estimates alone do not provide this additional context.

kp.k: Aggregate benchmark scores conceal task and language differences
kp.d: BIG-Bench Hard tasks show substantially different variance patterns, while Global-MMLU Lite language/category subdivisions consistently show strong item clustering. The tested systems score slightly higher on English questions, and English subdivisions tend to have slightly higher difficulty variance and ICC, especially in Business and Medical categories. The authors interpret this as better and more deterministic English performance, while stressing that these variance statistics concern the evaluated system pool rather than necessarily describing an untested LLM.
qs: Reporting only a single aggregate score misses the opportunity to analyze differences between benchmark subdivisions such as task, category, or language.
suggesting that the tested LLMs not only perform better but also more deterministically in English.
If an LLM does not belong to the evaluated population, it may exhibit different behaviors.

kp.k: Generalization depends on representativeness and the sampling process
kp.d: Both estimation approaches require representative items for unbiased generalized-accuracy estimates and independent selection for valid uncertainty estimates. Actual benchmark construction often deliberately balances subjects and difficulty rather than sampling independently. The authors describe a tradeoff: broad, practically meaningful superpopulations may yield biased estimates, while narrowly defined populations can satisfy assumptions but limit relevance. Generalized accuracy does not remedy systematic prompt or formatting bias.
qs: Specifically, point estimates require that benchmark items are representative of the superpopulation for unbiasedness, while uncertainty estimates require independence.
In practice, benchmark items are typically not independently sampled.
Generalized accuracy captures some sources of random, non-systematic item variation, but not systematic sources of bias.
if all benchmark items use the same prompt template, then strictly speaking, generalized accuracy corresponds only to the superpopulation of items following that template.

kp.k: Single capability scores and small benchmarks impose limitations
kp.d: The GLMM assumes one scalar capability per LLM, one scalar difficulty per item, a logistic additive relationship, normally distributed difficulties and conditionally independent trials. Violating unidimensionality also challenges the interpretation of a single aggregate regression-free score. Very small benchmarks constrain both frequentist approaches; Bayesian methods may help but require appropriate priors. Experiments concern binary-scored multiple-choice questions, although the authors say the methods also apply to binary-scored open-ended items; alternative metrics such as pass@k may need different models.
qs: Instead, a single score may reflect an arbitrary weighting of multiple distinct capabilities
A very small benchmark limits the usefulness of any frequentist method, including the GLMM and regression-free approaches described in this paper, especially when it comes to uncertainty estimation.
This paper also does not consider alternative item metrics such as pass@k, which in many cases require different statistical models for analysis.

kp.k: Extensions support comparisons, explanatory predictors and incomplete evaluations
kp.d: The authors identify applications not demonstrated in the experiments: statistical tests comparing system capability estimates; additional system, item or annotator predictors; and estimation with missing or imbalanced observations. They suggest a new LLM tested on only part of a previously evaluated benchmark could, under suitable conditions, receive predictions for overall and remaining-item performance. These are proposed extensions, not validated outcomes of the reported experiments.
qs: We briefly note some additional GLMM applications and extensions not illustrated in this work:
GLMMs enable principled comparison of LLM performance via statistical tests comparing estimated capabilities.
a GLMM can predict the new LLM’s overall benchmark or generalized accuracy, as well as accuracy on the remaining items.

kp.k: Evaluators should disclose assumptions and consider multiple models
kp.d: The authors recommend explicit statistical modeling rather than universally prescribing GLMMs. Benchmark accuracy and regression-free methods minimize assumptions but offer less generalization or explanation; generalized accuracy and GLMMs provide broader uncertainty accounting and potentially greater precision at the cost of additional assumptions. Reporting results under multiple statistical models may be appropriate.
qs: Ultimately, the statistical validity of LLM evaluations benefits from evaluators explicitly adopting a model for analyzing evaluation results — whether the GLMM, a regression-free model, or something else — and disclosing related assumptions.
In some cases, evaluators may want to report estimates from multiple statistical models.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Keller and co-authors argue that explicit statistical modeling can make AI benchmarking more reliable, informative and, under suitable conditions, more data-efficient. This is a cross-domain methodological source, not a prediction about legal services.
pts.d: The authors distinguish benchmark accuracy, which concerns a fixed set of tested items, from generalized accuracy, which concerns a superpopulation of similar items. They argue that this distinction changes the uncertainty that must be reported and can change conclusions about differences between LLMs. They warn that treating repeated trials as independent produces overly large uncertainty estimates for benchmark accuracy and overly small ones for generalized accuracy. Their principal empirical claim is that well-specified generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) produce generalized accuracy estimates similar to regression-free methods while often yielding narrower, more stable confidence intervals. They infer that evaluators may therefore need fewer costly trials or benchmark items. They also claim that estimated item difficulties and variance decomposition reveal benchmark problems and differences in LLM behavior hidden by aggregate scores. Additional applications, presented as possibilities rather than demonstrated findings, include incorporating explanatory predictors and predicting performance on untested items from incomplete evaluations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on mathematical derivations, simulations and evaluations of 22 API-access LLMs on three benchmarks; cost reductions and proposed extensions are methodological implications rather than directly measured deployment outcomes.
pts.d: The authors derive estimators and uncertainty formulas and compare GLMM and regression-free methods in three simulated settings: a well-specified logistic process, a linear probability process, and a process without shared latent structure. Table 8 reports baseline mean confidence-interval widths of 0.153 for GLMM versus 0.165 for regression-free estimates, with coverage of 0.940 versus 0.946 for nominal 95% intervals and similar RMSE. In the no-structure setting, Table 7 reports GLMM coverage of 0.867 versus 0.952 for regression-free estimates. The real evaluations use GPQA-Diamond, BIG-Bench Hard and Global-MMLU Lite, with eight trials per GPQA item and five per item on the other benchmarks. GPQA-Diamond contains 198 items. Their GPQA analysis finds similar point estimates and mostly narrower GLMM intervals. Item analysis identifies an ambiguously worded BIG-Bench Hard date question that all tested LLMs failed. GPQA chemistry questions have higher estimated difficulty than biology and physics questions, while human difficulty labels have only a weak relationship with LLM difficulty. Variance decomposition finds substantial differences across BIG-Bench Hard tasks and generally strong item clustering in Global-MMLU Lite. The source also draws on established hierarchical modeling and psychometric literature. It does not measure legal work, enterprise savings or downstream adoption outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The February 2026 publication makes present methodological claims and conditional proposals, without a dated forecast of future AI capability or adoption.
pts.d: The efficiency claim is conditional on adequate statistical specification, with benefits generally greater for smaller benchmarks and potentially larger tested LLM pools; gains diminish as benchmark size increases. Generalized accuracy requires representative items for unbiased point estimates and independent item selection for valid uncertainty estimates. It does not establish unrestricted real-world generalization or remove systematic prompt and selection biases. The GLMM additionally assumes scalar capability and difficulty, a logistic relationship with equal item discrimination, and normally distributed item difficulties. Both methods require appropriate conditional independence of trials. The authors acknowledge degraded GLMM coverage under substantial misspecification and limitations of any frequentist method on very small benchmarks. Experiments concern multiple-choice, binary-scored items using the tested systems' evaluation configurations; extensions to open-ended binary-scored tasks are proposed as applicable, while other scoring schemes may require different statistical models. Predictions from missing or imbalanced data are expressly conditional. The dates of the evaluation runs are not specified in the supplied text.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are AI evaluators, benchmark designers, developers and procurers in research and enterprise settings.
pts.d: Evaluators gain methods for distinguishing performance estimands, quantifying uncertainty, comparing systems and deciding whether to spend evaluation resources on additional trials or additional unique items. Benchmark designers gain item-difficulty estimates and diagnostics that may identify ambiguous questions, unequal domain difficulty and heterogeneous benchmark subdivisions. Developers and procurers are downstream users of more interpretable evidence for development and adoption decisions. Findings about language differences are limited to the tested LLM pool: the authors suggest that these systems perform better and more deterministically in English on the examined Global-MMLU Lite subdivisions. No legal profession segment, law firm, client group or access-to-justice population is studied, and the source does not claim that improved benchmarking itself improves underlying LLM capability.
